title: What Mehandi gold plating and antique finish mean
description: Mehandi gold, antique, matte and Rajwadi finishes explained: how each looks, which outfits they suit, and how to care for darker gold-tone jewellery.
intro: Mehandi gold plating is a deep, dark gold finish with a slightly olive-brown tint, named because it resembles the colour of dried mehendi on the hands. Antique finish is a broader term for any gold tone that has been darkened to look aged, usually with blackened grooves and softer highlights. Both are chosen to make fashion jewellery look like an heirloom rather than something brand new and shiny.

sections.heading: How these finishes are created
paragraphs: Most darker gold finishes start the same way as any gold-plated piece: a brass or alloy base is plated with a gold layer. The difference comes afterwards. The surface is then treated so that it darkens, either through a chemical darkening step, a tinted coating, or a combination, and the raised parts may be lightly brushed back so the design stands out.
Methods vary from one workshop to another, and sellers rarely share exact recipes. What matters for you as a buyer is how the finish looks in daylight and whether it is evenly applied.

sections.heading: A quick guide to the finishes you will see
paragraphs: Product listings use many names for gold tones. These are the most common, described as they are generally used in Indian fashion jewellery:
list: Mehandi gold: dark, matte, with a greenish or brownish undertone. Very popular on Kundan and Rajasthani designs.
Antique gold: darker than bright gold, with blackened recesses that highlight carving and figure work. Common in temple jewellery.
Matte gold: soft and non-reflective, but without the dark tint of mehandi or antique.
Rajwadi finish: a rich, deep, slightly warm gold that aims for a royal, vintage look. The term is used loosely, so compare photos.
High or bright gold: the shiny, yellow, mirror-like finish most people picture when they think of gold plating.

sections.heading: Why people choose a darker gold
paragraphs: There are practical reasons, not just style. Bright gold plating can look obviously new and sometimes a little brassy in harsh daylight. Darker finishes have a quieter, more expensive feel, which is why many brides and their families prefer them for photographs.

They are also forgiving. Minor rubbing on a bright gold piece shows quickly because the surface is mirror-smooth. On a mehandi or antique piece, small changes in tone blend into the overall aged look, so the jewellery keeps looking good for longer.
Finally, darker gold makes stones pop. Red, green and white Kundan stones look richer against a muted base than against high-shine gold.

sections.heading: Matching the finish to your outfit
paragraphs: Mehandi and antique gold love deep, warm colours: maroon, wine, bottle green, rust, mustard and royal blue. They also sit beautifully with heavy zari and zardozi, because they do not fight with the shine of the embroidery.

With pastels such as mint, powder pink or ivory, a matte or lighter antique gold often looks softer and more balanced than a very dark mehandi tone. Bright gold, on the other hand, can look striking with plain silk or a solid-coloured saree where the jewellery is meant to be the main shine.

Try to keep one gold tone across a single look. A mehandi necklace with bright gold bangles can make one of them look off. If you are shopping for a full bridal look, it helps to buy the necklace, earrings and maang tikka from the same set, or check finishes in daylight before the function. You can see a range of gold-tone styles in Varaha's [bridal jewellery](/women/bridal-jewellery) section.

sections.heading: What to check when buying online
paragraphs: Darker finishes are harder to photograph accurately. Indoor lighting can make mehandi gold look almost brown, while bright light can make it look like normal gold. Look for product photos taken in natural light, and check customer photos if available.

When the piece arrives, see it near a window. The finish should be even across the front and back, with no shiny bare patches or sticky spots. If it is very different from what you expected, use the return window: Varaha, for instance, offers 7-day returns.

sections.heading: Caring for mehandi and antique finishes
paragraphs: Do not try to 'clean' a dark finish to make it brighter. Polishing cloths with chemicals, toothpaste, lemon or gold-cleaning liquids can strip the darkened layer and leave patchy bright spots. A soft, dry, plain cotton or microfiber cloth is all you need.

Keep the pieces away from water and perfume, store them in separate pouches, and lay heavy necklaces flat. Over time, the raised areas may become slightly lighter from wear, which many people actually like, since it adds to the antique feel.

faq.q: What is mehandi polish in jewellery?
faq.a: It is a dark, matte gold finish with a greenish-brown tint, resembling the colour of dried mehendi. It gives fashion jewellery an heirloom look.

faq.q: Is antique finish jewellery real gold?
faq.a: Usually not in fashion jewellery. It is a gold-plated base metal that has been darkened for an aged appearance.
It can lighten slightly on raised areas over time, but darker finishes generally hide wear better than bright gold.

faq.q: Can I clean antique jewellery with toothpaste?
faq.a: No. Toothpaste is abrasive and can strip the darkened finish. Use only a soft dry cloth.
